extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for forming, classifying, and judging the validity and value of syllogisms, ratiocination, and induction as modes of inference in logic and scientific reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent requirements for a legitimate syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: To a legitimate syllogism it is essential that there should be three, and no more than three, propositions (the conclusion and two premises) and three, and no more than three, terms (the subject and predicate of the conclusion and a middle term). The middle term must be found in both premises; the major premise contains the middle and the major term, the minor premise contains the middle and the minor term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic structural requirement: exactly three propositions and exactly three terms, with the middle term linking the premises. Examples: All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal. The major/minor distinction is determined by the location of the major and minor terms relative to the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification into figures by middle-term position
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms are divided into figures according to the position of the middle term: subject in both premises, predicate in both, or subject in one and predicate in the other (first, second, third figures; a fourth figure is sometimes recognized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most common: middle term is subject of major and predicate of minor (first figure). The same argument may be expressed more naturally in a different figure even though it is logically equivalent; the figure is a means of classifying forms, not of changing their logical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moods determined by quantity and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Each figure is divided into moods according to the quantity (universal or particular) and quality (affirmative or negative) of the propositions. Only certain combinations (moods) are legitimate—i.e., the conclusion correctly follows from the premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives explicit exemplars of all legitimate moods for the four figures (e.g., First Figure: All B is C / All A is B -> All A is C; No B is C / All A is B -> No A is C; etc.). Legitimacy is judged by whether, given true premises, the conclusion must inevitably be true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity criterion: truth of premises implies inevitable truth of conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A syllogism is legitimate only if, when the premises are true, the conclusion must inevitably be true. If there is anything in the conclusion not already asserted or implied by the premises, the syllogism is vicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classic logical standard of validity. The author emphasizes that although syllogisms cannot prove more than is involved in the premises (petitio principii), they can still serve as reasoning devices to make implicit content explicit and to exhibit the grounds of belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to the first figure (rules for conversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: All correct ratiocination admits of being stated in syllogisms of the first figure alone; arguments in other figures may be reduced to the first by conversion or conversion per accidens of one or other premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: convert a universal negative (No C is B) to No B is C to reduce a 2nd-figure syllogism to the 1st. For a universal affirmative (All B is A) conversion per accidens yields Some A is B. Reduction shows that differences between figures are largely linguistic rather than logical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of generality: Induction vs Ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is inferring a proposition more general than the premises (inferring from less-general to more-general); Ratiocination (syllogism) infers a proposition equally or less general than the premises. When the conclusion is more general than the largest premise, call it Induction; when less general or equally general, call it Ratiocination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This offers a working taxonomy of types of inference based on the comparative generality of conclusion and premises. The author notes that induction and certain forms of combining general propositions are substantially the same process and that induction will be treated in more detail elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major premise universality and minor premise affirmativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: In the two general first-figure forms the major premise is a universal proposition, and the other premise (the minor) is always affirmative, asserting that the subject belongs to the class of the major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this arrangement, the character (affirmative/negative) of the major determines that of the conclusion. Practical formulation: 'Attribute A is a mark of attribute B; the given object has mark A; therefore it has attribute B.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions must assert factual relations, not mere verbal classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition which conveys real information asserts a matter of fact dependent on the laws of nature (e.g., that an object possesses an attribute or that two attributes co-exist), not merely the meaning of words or class membership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes views (e.g., Hobbes) that reduce propositions to verbal conventions. For syllogistic reasoning to have cognitive value, its premises must state factual co-occurrences or incompatibilities—otherwise the syllogism is merely a verbal or classificatory exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental axioms grounding syllogistic legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Two factual axioms underlie legitimate syllogisms: (1) For affirmative syllogisms: 'things which co-exist with the same thing, co-exist with one another' (transitive co-existence). (2) For negative syllogisms: 'a thing which co-exists with another thing, with which other a third thing does not co-exist, is not co-existent with that third thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axioms relate to facts, not to conventions, and are the ground of legitimacy in any argument where facts (not mere definitions) are the matter treated of. They may be seen as analogous to mathematical axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogism as practical 'mark' formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Every syllogism can be phrased as: 'Attribute A is a mark of attribute B; the given object has mark A; therefore the given object has attribute B.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reformulation emphasizes the practical/evidential role of syllogisms: using observed marks as evidence for attributes. It helps translate speculative general propositions into practical inference rules for recognizing properties in individual cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as a genuine inference extending beyond observed instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is a real process of inference: the conclusion in an induction embraces more than is contained in the premises. A principle ascertained by experience is a generalization expressive of our belief that what was found true in observed cases is true in an indefinite number of unobserved cases, including future facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion highlights that induction justifies belief about unobserved or future instances on the basis of observed ones, and that its legitimacy depends on conditions (to be examined elsewhere) which make such generalization warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of petitio principii and the epistemic role of syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Although every syllogism contains petitio principii (the conclusion is already somehow involved in the premises), syllogisms can still be informative to a person because they unfold and make explicit assertions 'wrapped up' or implied in premises, thereby bringing out the full force of what has been admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both a limitation and a function of syllogistic reasoning: it cannot create new factual content beyond premises, but it can render implicit content explicit, clarify grounds, and make consequences perceptible—an important role in mathematical and scientific exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical value: logical axioms and training in careful assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Listing elementary logical generalizations (axioms) and practicing logical exposition cultivates habits of circumspect interpretation of words and of precisely measuring the length and breadth of assertions—conditions indispensable to considerable mental attainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though axioms may seem obvious or redundant, presenting them serves as training for students to apprehend general truths and to develop disciplined habits needed in rigorous thought and scientific inquiry.
